  Terse gloss: "Entrance, doorway; the setting of the sun (westward); the act of coming in or arriving"
  Readable gloss: "A noun derived from the root bo' (to come, enter), mavo' denotes the place where one enters -- a gate, doorway, or passage into a building or city (Judg 1:24; 2 Kgs 11:16). When paired with shemesh (sun), it takes on a directional meaning: the place where the sun 'enters' the horizon, i.e., the west or sunset (Ps 50:1; 104:19). Spanish 'puesta de sol' and French 'coucher de soleil' both capture this sunset sense distinctly from the architectural meaning. Occasionally it functions as a verbal noun describing the act of arriving or entering (Ezek 33:31)."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "entrance or doorway"
    Enriched: The physical entrance or doorway into a defined space -- a city gate (Judg 1:24-25), a temple threshold (2 Kgs 16:18), or a guardroom passage (1 Chr 9:19). English glosses 'entrance of' and Spanish 'entrada de' consistently render this spatial, architectural sense across translations.
    Existing Spanish translations: [kethiv], a-entrada-de, en-la-entrada, entrada, entrada-de, la-entrada, por-la-entrada
  Sense 2: "setting of the sun"
    Enriched: The going-down or setting of the sun, and by extension the direction west. Psalm 50:1 pairs 'from the rising of the sun to its mavo'' as a merism for all the earth. French 'coucher de' and Spanish 'puesta de' highlight the astral meaning that English 'entrance of' can obscure.
    Existing Spanish translations: entrada-del, la-entrada-de, puesta-de, puesta-suya, su-ocaso
  Sense 3: "act of coming in"
    Enriched: The act or event of coming in, used as a verbal noun. In 2 Samuel 3:25 Abner's 'coming in and going out' is scrutinized as intelligence; in Ezekiel 33:31 the people's 'coming' to the prophet is habitual. Spanish 'entrada tuya' (your entering) preserves the active, processual quality.
    Existing Spanish translations: (entrada-tuya), [entrada-tuya], como-entradas-de, como-venir-de
